title: Chapter 4 Drill: Medical and Surgical Complications of Pregnancy

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar disorder takes lithium and is stable. She is 6 weeks pregnant. Which statement about management is correct?
options: Lithium should be stopped at once because it causes neural tube defects
Dose requirements fall in pregnancy and rise abruptly after delivery
Clearance rises, so levels and dose need close monitoring
Levels need not be checked once the first trimester is complete
items.explanation: Lithium is associated with a small absolute increase in Ebstein anomaly, but abrupt discontinuation risks relapse. Renal clearance rises during pregnancy and falls abruptly after delivery, so levels are monitored and the dose adjusted throughout, with extra care in the postpartum period. Neural tube defects are a valproate concern. Requirements rise rather than fall in pregnancy, and monitoring continues beyond the first trimester.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1c of 9.4 percent asks about becoming pregnant. Which counseling is most appropriate?
options: Conceive now because insulin can be adjusted later
Optimize control first and start folic acid
Stop insulin to avoid fetal exposure
Wait until the second trimester to optimize control
items.explanation: Hyperglycemia during organogenesis raises the risk of cardiac and neural tube defects, and the risk rises with the hemoglobin A1c. Control should be optimized before conception, with a target below 6 percent when achievable without significant hypoglycemia, along with folic acid. Insulin does not cross the placenta meaningfully and is not stopped. Control in the second trimester comes after the embryo has already been exposed.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 26 weeks will undergo laparoscopic surgery for an ovarian torsion. Which fetal monitoring plan is most appropriate?
options: Fetal heart rate documented before and after the operation
Continuous monitoring is mandatory for every case
No monitoring is acceptable before viability
Daily ultrasonography for fetal movement for a week
items.explanation: Once the fetus is viable, fetal heart rate is checked before and after the procedure, and intraoperative monitoring is individualized according to the procedure and gestational age. Mandatory continuous monitoring is not required and may interfere with the operation. Postoperative checks are appropriate at this age. Daily ultrasonography to count movements is neither practical nor supported.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 18 weeks, who has never had chickenpox, was exposed to her nephew with active varicella two days ago. Varicella IgG is negative. What is the best management?
options: Intravenous acyclovir starting immediately
Live varicella vaccine today
Reassurance with no treatment unless a rash appears
Varicella zoster immune globulin within 10 days of exposure
items.explanation: A susceptible pregnant woman exposed to varicella receives varicella zoster immune globulin within 10 days to reduce maternal disease. Acyclovir is reserved for those who develop pneumonia or disease. The vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. Waiting for a rash forgoes prevention, and maternal varicella pneumonia carries significant mortality. Congenital varicella includes limb hypoplasia, scarring, and chorioretinitis.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 woman with type 1 diabetes at 30 weeks has had vomiting for two days and received betamethasone yesterday. Glucose is 190 mg/dL, pH is 7.15, bicarbonate is 10 mEq/L, and serum ketones are positive. The fetal tracing shows minimal variability. What is the best initial management?
options: Immediate cesarean delivery to improve fetal status
Fluids, insulin infusion, and potassium as needed
Subcutaneous insulin and oral hydration
Sodium bicarbonate infusion without insulin
items.explanation: Ketoacidosis in pregnancy occurs at glucose levels below 200 mg/dL, and corticosteroids or vomiting can trigger it. Treatment is fluids, an insulin infusion, and potassium replacement, adding dextrose when glucose falls. Fetal heart rate abnormalities improve as maternal acidosis is corrected, so urgent delivery is not the response. Subcutaneous insulin is inadequate for acidosis, and bicarbonate alone leaves the ketosis uncorrected.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G3P1 woman with a body mass index of 38 and gestational diabetes in her last pregnancy presents at 9 weeks for her first prenatal visit. Which approach to glucose screening is best?
options: Test now, then repeat at 24 to 28 weeks if normal
Defer all testing until 24 to 28 weeks
Test only if glucose appears in the urine
Obtain a fasting glucose at 36 weeks
items.explanation: Women with obesity or prior gestational diabetes are screened at the first visit, because unrecognized pregestational diabetes is likely in this group and affects organogenesis. Standard nonpregnant criteria are used early, and a normal result is repeated at 24 to 28 weeks. Waiting until the routine window misses early disease. Glycosuria is nonspecific in pregnancy, and a test at 36 weeks is too late for therapy to help.

items.stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 35 weeks asks when she will be tested for group B streptococcus carriage. When is screening performed?
options: At the first prenatal visit only
At 28 weeks with the glucose screen
At 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks of gestation
On admission in active labor only
items.explanation: Group B streptococcus colonization is screened by vaginal and rectal culture at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks, a window chosen to predict status at delivery. Testing at the first visit or at 28 weeks is too early because colonization changes. Testing only in labor does not allow culture-based decisions and is reserved for women with unknown status.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P1 woman, three days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth, returns with a severe headache. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mm Hg on repeat measurement. She had normal pressures throughout pregnancy and labor. What is the best management?
options: Acetaminophen and reassessment in one week
Magnesium and an intravenous antihypertensive
Epidural blood patch
Sumatriptan and outpatient follow up
items.explanation: Blood pressure peaks three to six days after delivery, and postpartum preeclampsia can appear up to six weeks after birth. Severe-range pressure with headache calls for magnesium sulfate and treatment within 30 to 60 minutes. Simple analgesia and delay risk stroke or eclampsia. A blood patch treats a postdural puncture headache, which does not raise pressure. A triptan is a vasoconstrictor and is inappropriate with severe hypertension.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and is found to be 7 weeks pregnant. Which fetal condition is most specifically associated with warfarin exposure at this stage?
options: Warfarin embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia
Ebstein anomaly with right ventricular atrialization
Neural tube defects and caudal regression syndrome
Aplasia cutis congenita with choanal atresia
items.explanation: Warfarin crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy when taken between about 6 and 12 weeks, producing nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses. Ebstein anomaly is linked to lithium. Neural tube defects follow valproate or uncontrolled diabetes, and caudal regression follows diabetes. Aplasia cutis and choanal atresia are signs of methimazole embryopathy. Because valve thrombosis is also dangerous, the regimen is planned with cardiology.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 30 weeks is treated for secondary syphilis with benzathine penicillin. Four hours later she has fever, chills, uterine contractions, and decreased fetal movement with a late deceleration on the tracing. What is the most likely cause?
options: Penicillin anaphylaxis
Chorioamnionitis from ascending infection
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
Placental abruption
items.explanation: Treatment of syphilis can release spirochete products, causing fever, contractions, and fetal heart rate changes within hours, known as the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Treatment is supportive, and penicillin is continued. Anaphylaxis would present with hives, wheeze, and hypotension. Chorioamnionitis requires ruptured membranes or long labor and uterine tenderness. Abruption presents with bleeding and pain rather than fever following treatment.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 16 weeks has confirmed primary toxoplasmosis acquired two weeks ago. Amniocentesis polymerase chain reaction is negative. What is the best therapy?
options: Pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid
Observation without treatment
Intravenous acyclovir
Spiramycin to reduce transmission
items.explanation: When maternal toxoplasmosis is confirmed and the fetus is not known to be infected, spiramycin reduces transmission. Pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine plus folinic acid is used when fetal infection is documented. Observation misses the chance to lower transmission, and acyclovir treats herpesviruses rather than this parasite. The classic fetal triad is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 woman at 12 weeks smokes half a pack of cigarettes a day. She says she cannot quit. What is the best approach at every prenatal visit?
options: Advise that light smoking is safe in pregnancy
Report her to child protective services
Offer cessation counseling and behavioral support
Stop prenatal care until she quits
items.explanation: Tobacco cessation counseling is offered at every visit, because smoking increases abruption, growth restriction, stillbirth, and preterm birth, and no level of smoking is safe. Behavioral support is the foundation, with pharmacotherapy considered when it fails. Reassuring her is incorrect. Substance use is managed with treatment rather than punishment, and withholding care removes the setting where help is offered.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 32 weeks has pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Heart rate is 112 beats per minute and oxygen saturation is 93 percent on room air. Her chest radiograph is normal, and compression ultrasonography of both legs is negative. Which test is most appropriate next?
options: A D-dimer level to exclude pulmonary embolism
A transthoracic echocardiogram to exclude a clot
Repeat chest radiography in 48 hours
Ventilation and perfusion scintigraphy
items.explanation: With a normal chest radiograph and no leg findings, a ventilation and perfusion scan or computed tomographic angiography is the correct pathway, and both deliver fetal radiation well below the harm threshold. The normal radiograph favors scintigraphy. D-dimer is normally elevated in pregnancy and cannot exclude embolism. Echocardiography may show strain but does not exclude clot. Delay risks death from an untreated embolus.

items.stem: A woman with severe, uncorrected mitral stenosis and pulmonary hypertension desires continued pregnancy. At which point is she at greatest risk of acute decompensation?
options: Immediately after delivery
At 8 weeks, when the embryonic heart begins to beat
In the early second trimester, when blood volume starts to rise
At 6 weeks postpartum, when menses usually return
items.explanation: Blood volume peaks at about 30 to 34 weeks, and cardiac output surges around delivery as uterine contraction returns blood to the maternal circulation, so decompensation clusters at those points and in the first hours after birth. Early pregnancy and the start of the second trimester place far smaller loads on the heart. By six weeks postpartum, volume and output have largely returned to baseline.

items.stem: A 36-year-old G4P3 woman at 36 3/7 weeks with preeclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. Blood pressure is 172/114 mm Hg and is unchanged 20 minutes later on repeat measurement. Which treatment is appropriate within the next hour?
options: Oral lisinopril, starting at a low dose
Intravenous labetalol, given in repeated doses as needed
Oral methyldopa, repeated every six hours
Intravenous nitroprusside as the first-line agent
items.explanation: Persistent severe-range pressure is treated within 30 to 60 minutes to prevent stroke, using intravenous labetalol, intravenous hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors injure the fetal kidney. Methyldopa acts too slowly for an acute crisis and is a maintenance drug for chronic hypertension. Nitroprusside risks fetal cyanide toxicity and is reserved for refractory cases.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 32 weeks is hypotensive after a motor vehicle collision. Blood pressure falls to 78/40 mm Hg when she is supine on a backboard and rises to 104/62 mm Hg when she is tilted. Which maneuver is most appropriate?
options: Placing her in the Trendelenburg position
Placing her supine with the legs elevated
Manual or tilt-based left uterine displacement
Placing her in the right lateral position
items.explanation: After about 20 weeks the gravid uterus compresses the aorta and vena cava in the supine position, reducing venous return and cardiac output. Left lateral tilt or manual left uterine displacement relieves the compression, and maternal resuscitation is the best fetal therapy. Trendelenburg and leg elevation do not displace the uterus. The right lateral position displaces the uterus toward the vena cava and worsens compression.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who had gestational diabetes treated with insulin delivered a healthy infant yesterday. Her glucose values are now normal without insulin. Which follow-up plan is best?
options: A random glucose at six months postpartum
No testing, because insulin was stopped and values are normal
A hemoglobin A1c at two weeks postpartum
A 75 g glucose tolerance test at 4 to 12 weeks
items.explanation: Gestational diabetes confers a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, so persistent diabetes or prediabetes is sought with a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test between 4 and 12 weeks after delivery, followed by testing at least every three years. Normal values immediately after the placenta is delivered do not exclude later disease. A random glucose is insensitive, and the hemoglobin A1c is unreliable shortly after delivery.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 20 weeks has fatigue. She eats a restricted diet without fresh vegetables and takes no prenatal vitamin. Hemoglobin is 9.2 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume is 112 fL. The smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils, ferritin is normal, and serum folate is low. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Folic acid supplementation
Oral iron supplementation
Monthly intramuscular vitamin B12
Recombinant erythropoietin
items.explanation: Macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils and a low folate level indicates folate deficiency, which responds to folic acid. Iron would be correct for a microcytic picture with low ferritin, which she does not have. Vitamin B12 deficiency can look similar, but her dietary history and measured folate point away from it. Erythropoietin is not used for nutritional anemia because replacing the missing nutrient corrects the cause.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with generalized epilepsy controlled on valproate monotherapy plans pregnancy. What is the best recommendation?
options: Continue valproate at the lowest dose, since seizure control is the priority
Stop all antiseizure medication when pregnancy is confirmed
Change to lamotrigine or levetiracetam before conception
Add a second drug to allow a lower dose of valproate
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects, other malformations, and impaired neurodevelopment, so it is avoided in women of reproductive age whenever another drug controls the seizures. Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have lower malformation rates. The change should be made before conception, with folic acid started. Stopping all drugs risks dangerous seizures. Polytherapy raises malformation risk, so monotherapy is preferred.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with primary hypothyroidism takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily and has a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone. Her home test shows she is about 5 weeks pregnant. What is the best next step?
options: Continue the same dose and check thyroid-stimulating hormone at 20 weeks
Raise the dose 25 to 30 percent and recheck in four weeks
Stop levothyroxine until the end of the first trimester to protect the embryo
Add liothyronine to the current dose and check levels after delivery
items.explanation: Levothyroxine requirements rise by roughly 25 to 30 percent early in pregnancy, so a treated woman increases the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, with thyroid-stimulating hormone rechecked every four weeks in the first half. Waiting until 20 weeks permits months of undertreatment, which harms fetal neurocognitive development. Stopping therapy is dangerous. Liothyronine does not cross the placenta well and is not used.

items.stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the waiting room of the obstetric clinic. Once she is turned onto her left side and the airway is secured, which medication is the best choice to treat and prevent further seizures?
options: Phenytoin by intravenous loading dose
Lorazepam by intravenous injection
Levetiracetam by intravenous infusion
Magnesium sulfate by intravenous loading dose
items.explanation: Seizure in a woman with new hypertension after 20 weeks is eclampsia until proven otherwise. Magnesium sulfate is more effective than phenytoin or a benzodiazepine in both stopping and preventing recurrent seizures, and it is the drug of choice. Benzodiazepines may be used only if seizures persist despite magnesium. Phenytoin was inferior in randomized comparison, and levetiracetam is not the standard agent for eclampsia.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with chronic hypertension had a blood pressure of 130/84 mm Hg at her first visit. At 28 weeks it is 156/102 mm Hg, and urine protein to creatinine ratio is 0.6, up from 0.1 earlier. Platelets and creatinine are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Progression of chronic hypertension alone
Superimposed preeclampsia
Gestational hypertension
Preeclampsia with severe features
items.explanation: A rising pressure with new proteinuria in a woman who already has chronic hypertension indicates superimposed preeclampsia. Simple worsening of chronic disease does not produce new protein. Gestational hypertension is a diagnosis for women who were normotensive before 20 weeks. Severe features require a pressure of 160/110 or higher, or organ injury such as low platelets, rising creatinine, or pulmonary edema, none of which is present.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had a deep vein thrombosis during a prior pregnancy, and a first-degree relative also had a thrombosis. Testing is planned before a new pregnancy. Which inherited thrombophilia carries the highest risk of venous thromboembolism?
options: Antithrombin deficiency
Heterozygous factor V Leiden mutation
Heterozygous prothrombin gene mutation
Homozygous MTHFR C677T variant
items.explanation: Antithrombin deficiency is the strongest inherited thrombophilia for venous thromboembolism in pregnancy. Heterozygous factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations raise risk modestly. The MTHFR variant is not a thrombophilia in clinical practice, and testing for it is not recommended. Testing is useful mainly when the result changes management, as it would with a personal or first-degree family history of thrombosis, as in this patient.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with gestational diabetes at 29 weeks keeps a log showing fasting values of 105 to 112 mg/dL despite diet and exercise. Postprandial values are consistently within target. Which therapy best addresses her problem?
options: Short-acting insulin before each meal
Glyburide before breakfast
A further reduction in dietary carbohydrate at dinner
Intermediate-acting insulin at bedtime
items.explanation: Fasting hyperglycemia reflects overnight hepatic glucose output, and it is best treated with a bedtime intermediate-acting or long-acting insulin. Premeal short-acting insulin targets postprandial excursions, which are already controlled. Glyburide is no longer a preferred agent because of neonatal hypoglycemia and macrosomia. Further carbohydrate restriction has not helped after weeks of diet therapy and risks ketosis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 12 weeks has left calf swelling, and compression ultrasonography shows a femoral vein thrombosis. She starts therapeutic anticoagulation with an agent that does not cross the placenta. For how long should treatment continue?
options: Through pregnancy and six weeks postpartum
For three months in total, then stop even though she remains pregnant
Until 36 weeks, then stop so that neuraxial anesthesia can be offered
For six weeks, then switch to low-dose aspirin until delivery
items.explanation: Pregnancy-associated thrombosis is treated with therapeutic anticoagulation continued through the remainder of the pregnancy and for at least six weeks after delivery, with a minimum total duration of three months. Stopping at three months leaves a hypercoagulable pregnancy unprotected. Stopping at 36 weeks leaves the highest-risk period uncovered, and timed dosing intervals allow neuraxial anesthesia instead. Aspirin is not treatment for an established thrombosis.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 25 weeks attends her prenatal visit and is quiet, has bruises on her upper arms, and has missed several appointments. Which approach is best?
options: Ask in front of her partner to promote open communication
Screen only if she volunteers that she feels unsafe
Ask privately; offer safety planning and referral
Report to authorities without discussing it with her
items.explanation: Intimate partner violence often begins or escalates in pregnancy, and every patient should be screened, privately and with a validated approach. A positive screen is followed by safety planning and referral. Asking in front of a partner can endanger her. Screening only those who volunteer misses most victims. Reporting without discussion may break her trust and increase danger, though some jurisdictions have specific reporting laws.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has marked thirst, passes large volumes of dilute urine, and is diagnosed with diabetes insipidus. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Native vasopressin injections
Desmopressin
Fluid restriction alone
Intravenous hypertonic saline
items.explanation: Diabetes insipidus in pregnancy is treated with desmopressin, which is not degraded by placental vasopressinase. Native vasopressin is broken down by that enzyme, so it works poorly and is not the right choice. Restricting fluid in a patient who cannot concentrate urine risks dangerous dehydration. Hypertonic saline would worsen the high sodium that already accompanies the water loss. The disorder is rare, but the treatment is simple.

items.stem: A 22-year-old G1P0 woman at 10 weeks has a routine urine culture showing more than 100,000 colonies of Escherichia coli per milliliter. She has no dysuria, frequency, or fever. What is the best management?
options: Treat with a culture-directed antibiotic course
Observe, since she has no symptoms of urinary infection
Treat only if she later develops fever or flank pain
Repeat the culture at term and treat if still positive
items.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated in pregnancy because physiologic ureteral dilation lets untreated infection progress to pyelonephritis in a substantial proportion of women. The agent is chosen by culture sensitivity, and a repeat culture confirms cure. Waiting for symptoms or fever allows serious upper tract infection and possible sepsis. Deferring the culture to term exposes the patient to months of avoidable risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has anti-Ro antibodies and is 18 weeks pregnant. Which fetal complication is she at risk of, and what surveillance is offered?
options: Neural tube defects, with maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
Fetal thyroid goiter, with serial cervical length
Fetal anemia, with middle cerebral artery Doppler
Congenital heart block, with serial fetal PR interval measurement
items.explanation: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies cross the placenta and injure the fetal conduction system, causing congenital heart block, usually between 18 and 24 weeks. Surveillance of the fetal PR interval is offered. Neural tube defects are linked to valproate and diabetes. Goiter relates to antithyroid drugs or maternal thyroid disease, and fetal anemia surveillance with Doppler follows parvovirus or alloimmunization.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 2/7 weeks reports epigastric pain and nausea. Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Labs show platelets 68,000 per microliter, AST 220 U/L, LDH 800 U/L, and a peripheral smear with schistocytes. Fetal testing is reassuring. What is the best management?
options: Antenatal corticosteroids and delivery after 48 hours
Magnesium sulfate, then delivery once she is stable
Platelet transfusion and expectant management
Oral antihypertensive therapy with outpatient daily labs
items.explanation: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets define HELLP syndrome, which can occur with only mild hypertension. Delivery is the cure, and at 35 weeks nothing is gained by waiting, so magnesium is started for seizure prophylaxis and delivery follows stabilization. Corticosteroids are for fetal lung maturity before 34 weeks. Transfusion and expectant care risk hepatic rupture. Outpatient care is unsafe with active hemolysis.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman with known mitral stenosis is at 28 weeks and reports new exertional dyspnea. Heart rate is 118 beats per minute, there are no crackles, and oxygen saturation is normal. Which intervention best addresses the underlying problem?
options: Intravenous fluid boluses to raise preload across the narrowed valve
A dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker to reduce afterload and heart rate
A beta blocker to slow the heart rate
Early delivery by cesarean to relieve the volume load on the left atrium
items.explanation: In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastole and raises left atrial pressure, so symptoms appear as blood volume peaks. Heart rate control with a beta blocker is the central treatment. Fluid boluses worsen pulmonary congestion. Dihydropyridines cause reflex tachycardia and do not fit a fixed obstruction. Delivery is not needed for symptoms that respond to rate control, and cesarean adds hemodynamic stress.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with epilepsy takes lamotrigine at an unchanged dose and has been seizure-free for two years. At 20 weeks she has two breakthrough seizures despite good adherence. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Placental metabolism of the drug has made it ineffective
Prenatal vitamins have blocked absorption of lamotrigine
Fetal metabolism has removed the drug from circulation
Increased drug clearance has lowered her serum levels
items.explanation: Lamotrigine clearance rises markedly during pregnancy, so serum levels fall substantially and seizure control can be lost at a constant dose. The dose is adjusted according to clinical response and measured levels, and reduced again after delivery. The placenta and fetus do not account for this degree of loss, and prenatal vitamins do not block absorption of the drug in a clinically meaningful way.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and exertional syncope is 8 weeks pregnant. She asks about her options. Which counseling is most appropriate?
options: Continue the pregnancy with cardiology follow up and plan an uncomplicated vaginal delivery at term
Continue the pregnancy and give warfarin through gestation to prevent right heart thrombosis
Offer termination, given the extremely high risk
Reassure her that the risk is moderate and arrange monthly echocardiography as an outpatient
items.explanation: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is a modified World Health Organization class IV condition, in which pregnancy carries an extremely high risk of maternal death and is advised against. The patient should be offered termination, and if she continues, care in a center with a cardio-obstetrics team. Describing the risk as moderate is wrong. Warfarin is teratogenic and does not address the hemodynamic danger, and routine vaginal delivery plans underestimate the peripartum surge.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 12 weeks returns from travel to an area with Zika virus transmission and has no symptoms. Which counseling is most accurate?
options: Immediate termination because infection is certain
Evaluation and serial ultrasonography
No follow up is required without a rash
Amniocentesis for all returning travelers
items.explanation: Zika virus causes microcephaly and brain abnormalities, and women with possible exposure are evaluated and followed with serial ultrasonography according to current public health guidance. Infection is not certain and termination is not automatic. Many infections are asymptomatic, so absence of a rash does not exclude exposure. Amniocentesis is not routine for all travelers, and results would not change the surveillance plan.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine and plans to conceive within three months. Which advice is best?
options: Stop methotrexate before conception and continue hydroxychloroquine
Continue both drugs and stop methotrexate only if conception occurs
Stop hydroxychloroquine and continue methotrexate for disease control
Stop all medication, because disease usually worsens during pregnancy
items.explanation: Methotrexate and leflunomide are teratogenic and are stopped before conception, while hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and azathioprine are compatible with pregnancy. Waiting until conception exposes the embryo during early development. Hydroxychloroquine is the safe drug to keep. Rheumatoid arthritis often improves in pregnancy and flares postpartum, so stopping all treatment is not needed, and the active disease risks flares.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 14 weeks has acute appendicitis confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging. The surgeon proposes to wait until delivery to avoid harming the pregnancy. Which response is best?
options: Wait for delivery and give oral antibiotics until then
Operate only after 34 weeks when the fetus is viable
Proceed with appendectomy now, since delay raises risk of perforation
Give prophylactic tocolysis for two weeks before surgery
items.explanation: A woman who needs surgery should not be denied it because of pregnancy, since delay worsens outcomes. Perforation raises the risk of fetal loss and maternal sepsis. Waiting until delivery or viability is therefore unsafe. Appendectomy can be laparoscopic or open according to the surgeon, and prophylactic tocolysis is not required, so it does not justify postponing the operation.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 22 weeks has biliary colic and recurrent episodes, and ultrasonography confirms symptomatic cholecystitis with stones. She is febrile and has not improved on supportive care. Which approach is best?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the second trimester
Delay surgery until six weeks after delivery in all cases
Open cholecystectomy only because laparoscopy harms the fetus
Oral dissolution therapy for the duration of the pregnancy
items.explanation: Progesterone slows gallbladder motility and increases stone formation, and symptomatic cholecystitis that does not settle is treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy in any trimester when surgery is needed. Pregnancy is not a reason to withhold an operation, since delay increases complications. Open surgery is not required for fetal safety. Dissolution therapy is slow and unreliable for acute disease.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 weeks has intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. She takes ursodeoxycholic acid, and her peak serum bile acids are 112 micromoles per liter. When is delivery recommended?
options: 34 0/7 weeks
36 0/7 weeks
38 0/7 weeks
39 0/7 weeks
items.explanation: Bile acid concentrations of 100 micromoles per liter or more carry the highest risk of stillbirth, so delivery is recommended at 36 0/7 weeks. Earlier delivery at 34 weeks is considered only when liver disease is severe, itching is intractable, or the fetal status is nonreassuring. Delivery at 38 or 39 weeks suits milder disease with lower bile acid levels and would extend risk here.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P1 woman with severe preeclampsia delivered vaginally two hours ago. She received magnesium sulfate during labor, her creatinine is normal, and urine output is adequate. For how long should magnesium sulfate be continued after delivery?
options: 6 hours
48 hours
Until blood pressure falls below 140/90 mm Hg
24 hours
items.explanation: Seizure risk persists after delivery, and magnesium sulfate prophylaxis is generally continued for 24 hours postpartum in severe preeclampsia. Six hours is too short to cover the early postpartum period. Forty-eight hours adds exposure and toxicity risk without proven benefit. Blood pressure is not the endpoint, because seizures can occur at near normal pressures, and a pressure target does not define the duration.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman with moderate recurrent major depression asks for treatment at 10 weeks and plans to breastfeed. Which medication is the best choice?
options: Paroxetine as a new start
Valproate as a mood stabilizer
Sertraline
Lithium as monotherapy for depression
items.explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line for depression in pregnancy, and sertraline is often favored in breastfeeding women because infant exposure is low. Paroxetine has been linked to cardiac malformations and is generally avoided as an initial choice. Valproate is avoided for neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm. Lithium raises the risk of Ebstein anomaly and is not a treatment for unipolar depression.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has daily cough and wheeze, with nocturnal symptoms three times a week. She uses only an albuterol inhaler and has stopped her inhaled steroid because she fears fetal harm. What is the best advice?
options: Resume the inhaled corticosteroid as the preferred controller
Continue albuterol alone, because avoiding controller drugs protects the fetus
Replace it with a long-term course of oral prednisone for control
Use albuterol before bed and stop all controller therapy until delivery
items.explanation: Uncontrolled asthma carries greater fetal risk than the medications used to treat it, because maternal hypoxemia reduces fetal oxygen delivery. An inhaled corticosteroid is the preferred controller in pregnancy, with albuterol for symptoms. Relying on a reliever alone leaves persistent symptoms. Chronic oral steroids add systemic exposure unnecessarily, and withholding all controller therapy invites exacerbations during a pregnancy whose course is unpredictable.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 22 weeks of gestation has paroxysmal hypertension, pounding headaches, and sweating. A pheochromocytoma is confirmed biochemically. Which medical approach is correct before surgery?
options: A beta blocker alone to slow the rate
Alpha blockade before any beta blocker
A thiazide diuretic with sodium restriction
An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
items.explanation: A pheochromocytoma is treated with alpha blockade first, and beta blockade is added only afterward, because unopposed beta blockade can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. A beta blocker alone is therefore dangerous. A thiazide diuretic does not address catecholamine excess, and drugs that block the renin-angiotensin system are avoided in pregnancy. Surgery is planned once adequate blockade has been achieved.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 woman at 14 weeks has a throbbing unilateral headache with nausea that is consistent with her usual migraines. Neurologic examination and blood pressure are normal. Which treatment is first-line?
options: Ergotamine at the onset of the aura
Topiramate taken daily
Acetaminophen with an antiemetic
Valproate taken daily for prevention
items.explanation: Migraine often improves in pregnancy, and acetaminophen is first-line therapy, with an antiemetic when nausea is prominent. Triptans have reassuring observational data and may be used if needed. Ergot derivatives are contraindicated because they cause uterine vasoconstriction. Topiramate and valproate are avoided because of teratogenic risk, so preventive therapy, if required, uses an agent such as propranolol.

items.stem: A 24-year-old G1P0 woman at 24 weeks has two days of periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right upper abdomen, with anorexia and a temperature of 38.2 C. White cell count is 14,000 per microliter. Ultrasonography is nondiagnostic. What is the best next step?
options: Observation until the white cell count exceeds 20,000
Computed tomography only after the pregnancy ends
Empiric tocolysis and repeat examination next week
Magnetic resonance imaging of the abdomen
items.explanation: Appendicitis is the most frequent nonobstetric surgical emergency of pregnancy, and the appendix is displaced upward and laterally as the uterus enlarges. Ultrasonography is first-line, followed by magnetic resonance imaging when the result is unclear. Leukocytosis is normal in pregnancy and is not a reliable threshold. Delay increases the risk of perforation and fetal loss, and tocolysis is not a diagnostic or therapeutic plan.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, and well-controlled blood pressure is 9 weeks pregnant. Which measure most directly lowers her risk of preeclampsia?
options: Aspirin 81 mg daily
Vitamin C and vitamin E supplements every day
Bed rest at home from 28 weeks onward
Dietary sodium restriction below one gram daily
items.explanation: Renal disease is a high-risk factor for preeclampsia, growth restriction, and preterm birth. Low-dose aspirin started early, between 12 and 28 weeks and ideally before 16, reduces preeclampsia risk, and blood pressure and fetal growth are monitored closely. Antioxidant vitamins failed to prevent the disease in randomized trials. Bed rest and sodium restriction do not alter the incidence and bed rest raises thrombosis risk.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman at 29 weeks has confusion, fever, a platelet count of 22,000 per microliter, hemolysis with schistocytes, and creatinine 2.1 mg/dL. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg, and prothrombin time and fibrinogen are normal. What is the best treatment?
options: Magnesium sulfate and immediate delivery
Urgent plasma exchange
Platelet transfusion and high-dose antihypertensives
Intravenous immune globulin and observation
items.explanation: Microangiopathic hemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurologic signs, and normal coagulation studies without hypertension indicates thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which is distinguished from HELLP by those findings. Urgent plasma exchange is life-saving. Delivery with magnesium treats HELLP and does not reverse this disease. Transfusion may feed the thrombotic process. Immune globulin treats immune thrombocytopenia, not this condition.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 10 weeks uses heroin daily and wants to stop. She asks whether detoxification would protect the fetus. What is the best recommendation?
options: Supervised withdrawal over two weeks in hospital
Abrupt cessation with symptomatic care only
Naltrexone antagonist therapy started immediately
Maintenance therapy with buprenorphine or methadone
items.explanation: Opioid use disorder in pregnancy is treated with buprenorphine or methadone, because medically supervised withdrawal carries a high relapse risk and causes fetal stress. Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome is expected and treatable, and it is not a reason to avoid medication. Detoxification and abrupt cessation both risk relapse and overdose. Naltrexone is not standard in pregnancy and would precipitate withdrawal.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has a primary cytomegalovirus infection confirmed by serology. She asks what can be done to prevent fetal infection. What is the best counseling?
options: Hyperimmune globulin reliably prevents transmission
No intervention is proven to prevent transmission
Oral acyclovir eliminates the risk of fetal infection
Termination is mandatory because infection is certain
items.explanation: Cytomegalovirus is the most frequent congenital infection, and primary infection carries a higher transmission rate and more severe effects than reactivation. No intervention is proven to prevent transmission, and hyperimmune globulin is not recommended. Amniocentesis can confirm fetal infection, and hearing loss is the most common long-term sequela. Acyclovir has no role, and infection is not certain, so termination is not mandatory.

items.stem: A 29-year-old Rh-negative woman at 28 weeks sustained blunt abdominal trauma in a fall. She is stable and the fetal tracing is reassuring. Her antibody screen is negative. Which test best guides the dose of anti-D immune globulin?
options: Kleihauer-Betke test
Indirect Coombs titer
Apt test on vaginal fluid
Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein
items.explanation: Trauma can cause fetomaternal hemorrhage beyond the standard anti-D dose, and the Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetal red cells in the maternal circulation so that additional immune globulin can be given. The indirect Coombs titer detects maternal antibodies already formed and cannot size a hemorrhage. The Apt test distinguishes fetal from maternal blood in vaginal bleeding. Alpha-fetoprotein is a screening marker unrelated to dosing.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks has a platelet count of 118,000 per microliter on routine testing. Her blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, liver enzymes and creatinine are normal, and the smear is unremarkable. Platelets were normal at 12 weeks. What is the best management?
options: Corticosteroid therapy to raise the count
Plasma exchange for suspected thrombotic purpura
Induction of labor for suspected HELLP syndrome
Observation with a repeat count after delivery
items.explanation: Gestational thrombocytopenia is the most frequent cause, appears in the late second or third trimester, is mild, and resolves after delivery without treatment. Normal pressure, enzymes, creatinine, and smear argue against HELLP and microangiopathy. Steroids are given for immune thrombocytopenia with counts below 30,000 or bleeding. Plasma exchange is life-saving for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, which is not present here.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with Crohn disease takes sulfasalazine and has been in remission for a year. She is planning pregnancy. Which advice is correct?
options: Stop sulfasalazine before conception to avoid birth defects
Switch to methotrexate, which is safe in remission
Continue sulfasalazine and add folic acid supplementation
Defer conception until she has been off all therapy for a year
items.explanation: Disease activity at conception is the strongest predictor of poor outcome, so remission is maintained. Sulfasalazine, mesalamine, azathioprine, and biologic agents are generally continued, and folic acid is added for patients on sulfasalazine because it interferes with folate. Methotrexate is contraindicated in pregnancy. Stopping therapy risks a flare that harms the pregnancy more than the drug would.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 38 0/7 weeks has blood pressures of 148/92 and 150/94 mm Hg measured four hours apart in clinic. Urine protein to creatinine ratio is 0.1, platelets are 210,000 per microliter, creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL, and transaminases are normal. She feels well and the fetus is active. What is the best management?
options: Continue expectant management until 41 weeks
Start magnesium sulfate and deliver within 24 hours
Begin an antihypertensive and reassess in one week
Recommend induction of labor now
items.explanation: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or organ injury is gestational hypertension. Delivery is recommended at 37 0/7 weeks, and she has passed that point, so induction is appropriate. Waiting to 41 weeks ignores the delivery window. Magnesium sulfate is for severe features, which are absent. Medication and another week of waiting add risk without benefit because delivery is the definitive treatment at this gestational age.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 14 weeks has a reactive treponemal test and a titer of 1:32, with a history of anaphylaxis to penicillin. What is the best management?
options: Treat with doxycycline for 14 days
Treat with azithromycin in a single dose
Desensitize her and treat with penicillin G
Observe and retest in the third trimester
items.explanation: Penicillin G is the only therapy accepted for treating the fetus, so a woman with an allergy is desensitized rather than given another drug. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and azithromycin has documented failures, with inadequate fetal treatment. Observation leaves infection untreated, and untreated syphilis causes stillbirth and congenital disease. Early disease receives one dose of benzathine penicillin.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 20 weeks has uncomplicated cystitis. Her culture is sensitive to cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, fosfomycin, and ciprofloxacin. Which agent should be avoided?
options: Cephalexin
Ciprofloxacin
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Fosfomycin
items.explanation: Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy when safer alternatives exist, because of concerns about fetal cartilage and joint effects. Cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, and fosfomycin are acceptable options guided by sensitivity. Because several safe agents are active against her isolate, there is no reason to expose the fetus to a fluoroquinolone for a simple lower tract infection, and the choice should follow sensitivities.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G4P0 woman has had three consecutive losses at 8 weeks and has a persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two tests 12 weeks apart. She has never had a thrombosis and is now pregnant at 7 weeks. Which regimen is best?
options: Prophylactic-dose anticoagulation plus low-dose aspirin
Low-dose aspirin alone throughout pregnancy
Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation without aspirin
Prednisone throughout the first trimester
items.explanation: Obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome without prior thrombosis is treated with prophylactic-dose anticoagulation combined with low-dose aspirin, which improves live birth rates. Aspirin alone is less effective. Therapeutic-dose anticoagulation is reserved for women with a history of thrombosis. Corticosteroids do not improve outcomes in antiphospholipid syndrome and add maternal risks such as hyperglycemia and hypertension without benefit to the fetus.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with HIV taking combination antiretroviral therapy is at 37 weeks. Her most recent viral load is 5,200 copies per milliliter. What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Spontaneous labor with vaginal delivery planned
Scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine
Induction at 41 weeks with no further therapy
Cesarean after labor begins, without zidovudine
items.explanation: A viral load above 1,000 copies per milliliter near delivery prompts scheduled cesarean birth at 38 weeks and intravenous zidovudine to reduce perinatal transmission. Vaginal birth is appropriate only when the load is suppressed. Waiting until 41 weeks or after labor starts increases exposure to membrane rupture and labor. Omitting zidovudine removes a proven protective measure at the time of highest risk.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 28 weeks is hepatitis B surface antigen positive with a viral load of 8 million international units per milliliter. Which intervention reduces perinatal transmission further?
options: Antiviral therapy in the third trimester
Cesarean delivery for all hepatitis B carriers
Withholding breastfeeding after birth
Hepatitis B vaccination of the mother alone
items.explanation: When the maternal viral load is high, antiviral therapy in the third trimester is offered in addition to hepatitis B immune globulin and vaccine for the newborn. Cesarean delivery does not reduce transmission. Breastfeeding is permitted when the infant receives prophylaxis. Maternal vaccination does not help an infected carrier, and prophylaxis must be given to the neonate at birth.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 27 weeks has paroxysms of pounding headache, sweating, and palpitations with blood pressures to 210/120 mm Hg. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated and imaging shows an adrenal mass. Which medication should be started first?
options: A beta blocker as sole initial therapy
A diuretic to reduce the sodium load
An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
An alpha-adrenergic blocker
items.explanation: Pheochromocytoma causes catecholamine-driven paroxysmal hypertension. Alpha blockade comes first, and a beta blocker is added only afterward, because unopposed beta blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unchecked and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Diuretics worsen volume depletion in these patients. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy for fetal renal injury and do not block catecholamine effects.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman, six weeks after a delivery complicated by severe hemorrhage and transfusion, reports failure to lactate, persistent fatigue, and no return of menses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Peripartum cardiomyopathy
Postpartum thyroiditis in its hyperthyroid phase
Sheehan syndrome
Asherman syndrome from uterine curettage
items.explanation: Pituitary infarction after severe postpartum hemorrhage causes Sheehan syndrome, with failure of lactation, amenorrhea, and fatigue from loss of prolactin, gonadotropins, and other pituitary hormones. Peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with heart failure. The hyperthyroid phase of thyroiditis causes palpitations and weight loss, not failure of lactation. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhea but leaves lactation intact, because the pituitary is undamaged.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 kindergarten teacher at 22 weeks had a facial rash and arthralgia after an outbreak at school. Ultrasonography now shows fetal ascites and a thickened placenta. Which test best assesses fetal anemia?
options: Umbilical artery systolic to diastolic ratio
Biophysical profile score
Amniotic fluid index
Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
items.explanation: Parvovirus B19 suppresses fetal marrow and causes anemia that can progress to hydrops. Surveillance uses the middle cerebral artery Doppler, and severe anemia is treated with intrauterine transfusion. Umbilical artery Doppler assesses placental resistance in growth restriction, not anemia. The biophysical profile and amniotic fluid index describe fetal well-being and fluid but do not measure hemoglobin concentration.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with gestational diabetes requires insulin, has good glycemic control, normal growth with an estimated fetal weight of 3,400 g, and normal antenatal testing. When is delivery recommended?
options: 39 0/7 to 39 6/7 weeks
36 0/7 to 36 6/7 weeks
37 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks
40 0/7 to 40 6/7 weeks
items.explanation: For medication-controlled gestational diabetes with good control, delivery is recommended between 39 0/7 and 39 6/7 weeks. Earlier windows between 36 and 38 6/7 weeks are reserved for vascular disease, poor control, or a history of stillbirth. Waiting to 40 weeks is the option considered for diet-controlled disease, and it adds stillbirth risk when medication is needed. Cesarean is not indicated by weight below 4,500 g.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G3P2 woman at 36 weeks reports using cannabis daily throughout pregnancy to control nausea. She asks about effects on her infant. Which counseling is most accurate?
options: Cannabis is safe and may reduce nausea throughout pregnancy
The only risk is limited to the first trimester
It is linked to lower birth weight, so counsel cessation
Use is harmless if she avoids smoking it
items.explanation: Cannabis use in pregnancy is associated with lower birth weight, and patients should be counseled to stop, using a validated screening questionnaire given to every patient. It is not safe to treat as harmless or to assume that edible forms avoid the risk. Effects are not limited to early pregnancy, and the counseling is nonpunitive, offering support for cessation rather than judging her.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks undergoes a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. The fasting value is 94 mg/dL, the one-hour value is 170 mg/dL, and the two-hour value is 140 mg/dL. How should the result be interpreted?
options: Normal, because two abnormal values are required
Gestational diabetes, as one abnormal value suffices
Abnormal, and a three-hour 100 g test must confirm it
Diagnostic of overt diabetes mellitus
items.explanation: With the one-step 75 g test, the thresholds are 92 fasting, 180 at one hour, and 153 at two hours, and a single value at or above a threshold makes the diagnosis. The fasting value of 94 qualifies. The rule that two values are needed belongs to the two-step method. No confirmatory test follows the one-step diagnosis, and overt diabetes is defined by different criteria.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 33 weeks presents with sudden vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, and a firm tender uterus. Her urine drug screen is positive. Fetal heart tracing shows recurrent late decelerations. Which substance is most likely responsible?
options: Cocaine
Buprenorphine
Cannabis
Nicotine replacement
items.explanation: Cocaine causes vasoconstriction and sudden hypertension, and it is strongly associated with placental abruption, which fits sudden bleeding with a tender, firm uterus. Buprenorphine is a treatment, not a cause. Cannabis is associated with lower birth weight rather than abruption. Nicotine replacement carries lower risk than smoking, although tobacco smoking itself increases abruption and growth restriction.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 30 weeks has gestational diabetes diagnosed at 26 weeks. She follows her diet and checks glucose at home. Which fasting value is the standard target for glycemic control?
options: Below 70 mg/dL
Below 110 mg/dL
Below 95 mg/dL
Below 126 mg/dL
items.explanation: For gestational diabetes the fasting target is below 95 mg/dL, with one-hour postprandial values below 140 mg/dL or two-hour values below 120 mg/dL. A target below 70 would invite hypoglycemia and is not the goal. Thresholds of 110 and 126 are too permissive and correspond to values seen in overt diabetes, exposing the fetus to hyperglycemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension takes lisinopril and presents at 6 weeks of gestation after a positive pregnancy test. Her blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. What is the best next step in her management?
options: Continue lisinopril until the second trimester
Stop all antihypertensives and observe
Continue lisinopril and add folic acid
Change lisinopril to labetalol or nifedipine
items.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors cause fetal renal injury and oligohydramnios, so they are replaced when pregnancy is recognized. Labetalol and nifedipine are first-line alternatives, and methyldopa is another. Waiting to the second trimester exposes the fetus during a vulnerable period. Stopping all treatment is not needed with a pressure that is only controlled by drug. Folic acid does not offset the fetal renal effects.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G3P2 woman with moderate persistent asthma has atony and ongoing hemorrhage after delivery, and several uterotonic agents are available. Which should be avoided?
options: Intramuscular oxytocin infusion
Carboprost
Sublingual or rectal misoprostol
Methylergonovine intramuscularly
items.explanation: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2 alpha analog that can cause bronchospasm, so it is avoided in asthma. Oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic and is safe in asthma. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog that does not constrict bronchi. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic, not a uterotonic, but it carries no bronchospasm risk. Methylergonovine, though not offered here, is avoided in hypertension rather than asthma.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 20 weeks has a positive hepatitis C antibody test, and viremia is confirmed. She asks about treatment. What is the best advice?
options: Defer direct-acting antiviral treatment until after delivery
Start direct-acting antivirals now to prevent transmission
Plan cesarean delivery to avoid vertical transmission
Stop breastfeeding permanently after delivery
items.explanation: Hepatitis C is screened in every pregnancy, and direct-acting antiviral treatment is generally deferred until after delivery. Starting treatment now has not been shown to be safe, and the infant can be tested after birth. Cesarean delivery does not reduce transmission, which is low. Breastfeeding is allowed unless nipples are cracked and bleeding, so permanent cessation is unnecessary.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is at 30 weeks with new hypertension, proteinuria, and creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. Which finding most strongly supports a lupus flare over preeclampsia?
options: Elevated uric acid with right upper quadrant pain
Active urinary sediment with low complement levels
Thrombocytopenia with elevated liver enzymes
Headache that improves after delivery of the baby
items.explanation: A flare of lupus nephritis is separated from preeclampsia by an active urinary sediment with red cell casts, low complement levels, and rising anti-double-stranded DNA titers. Elevated uric acid, liver involvement, and thrombocytopenia occur in preeclampsia and HELLP. Improvement after delivery also suggests preeclampsia. The distinction matters because a flare is treated with immunosuppression rather than with delivery.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 weeks has right upper quadrant pain and headache. Blood pressure is 152/98 mm Hg, platelets are 78,000 per microliter, AST is 210 U/L, and LDH is 720 U/L. The smear shows schistocytes, and glucose and coagulation studies are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy
HELLP syndrome
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
items.explanation: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets with hypertension and right upper quadrant pain define HELLP syndrome. Acute fatty liver typically shows hypoglycemia, prolonged clotting times, and marked jaundice, which are absent here. Cholestasis causes itching with raised bile acids and no hemolysis or thrombocytopenia. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can mimic it, but hypertension at this gestation with liver injury and normal coagulation points to HELLP.

items.stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 woman with chronic hypertension takes lisinopril and has a positive pregnancy test at 6 weeks. Her blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Which change in therapy is most appropriate?
options: Continue lisinopril until the second trimester
Stop all treatment for the whole pregnancy
Change to atenolol for fetal protection
Switch to labetalol or nifedipine
items.explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are fetotoxic and should be replaced before or early in pregnancy, with labetalol or long-acting nifedipine being preferred. Continuing lisinopril into the second trimester risks fetal renal injury, oligohydramnios, and skull hypoplasia. Stopping all treatment is unnecessary at this level and leaves chronic hypertension unmonitored. Atenolol is associated with impaired fetal growth and is not preferred.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman, six weeks after delivery, has orthopnea and edema. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30 percent, and no other cause of heart failure is found. She is not breastfeeding and wants to know about future pregnancies. What is the best counseling?
options: Pregnancy is safe as long as she takes a diuretic daily from conception onward
Recurrence is rare, and she may conceive as soon as her symptoms resolve completely
Advise against another pregnancy while dysfunction persists
She may conceive after a year, since the recurrence risk is the same in every patient
items.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure with an ejection fraction below 45 percent appearing in the last month of pregnancy or within five months of delivery. Recurrence risk is high, and highest when the ejection fraction has not normalized, so women with persistent dysfunction are counseled against another pregnancy. Diuretics cannot prevent recurrence, and symptom resolution alone does not show recovery of function. The recurrence risk varies with recovery.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks with immune thrombocytopenia diagnosed before pregnancy has a platelet count of 24,000 per microliter and gum bleeding. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Platelet transfusion as scheduled prophylaxis
Prednisone or intravenous immune globulin
Splenectomy during the second trimester
Observation until the count falls below 10,000
items.explanation: Treatment of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy is started when platelets are below 30,000 per microliter or when there is bleeding, using corticosteroids or intravenous immune globulin. Scheduled transfusion is ineffective because the platelets are rapidly destroyed. Splenectomy is reserved for refractory cases, and waiting for a lower count is inappropriate in a woman who is already bleeding.

items.stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 30 weeks is brought to the emergency department after a low-speed car collision with a seat belt on. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness, normal vital signs, no bleeding, and no contractions. What is the best approach to fetal evaluation?
options: Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring for at least four hours
A single fetal heart rate check, then discharge
Immediate cesarean delivery to avoid abruption
Ultrasonography alone, with no tracing
items.explanation: Placental abruption is the main fetal threat after blunt abdominal injury and can occur after relatively minor force. For a viable pregnancy, monitoring continues for at least four hours, longer if contractions, bleeding, tenderness, or an abnormal tracing appear. A single check cannot exclude abruption, and ultrasonography is insensitive for it. Cesarean delivery is not indicated for a stable patient with a reassuring fetus.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 11 weeks had preeclampsia at 34 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her blood pressure today is 112/68 mm Hg and she takes no medication. Which counseling is most appropriate?
options: Begin aspirin only if blood pressure rises after 20 weeks
Start aspirin 325 mg daily at 20 weeks
No prophylaxis is indicated while pressures are normal
Start aspirin 81 mg daily now and continue until delivery
items.explanation: Prior preeclampsia is a high-risk factor, so low-dose aspirin is recommended, started between 12 and 28 weeks and ideally before 16. The dose is 81 mg daily, and it is given for prevention regardless of current pressure. Starting only after hypertension appears misses the preventive window. A 325 mg dose has no added benefit and raises bleeding risk. Normal pressure today does not remove the risk.
